bib.title: Agentic World Modeling: Foundations, Capabilities, Laws, and Beyond

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agentic World Modeling: Foundations, Capabilities, Laws, and Beyond", Meng Chu, Xuan Billy Zhang, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Lingdong Kong et al. (HKUST, NUS, Oxford, NTU and others; senior authors incl. Philip Torr, Jiaya Jia). arXiv:2604.22748v3, 16 Jun 2026. Preprint, "has not undergone peer review", described as position-driven survey. It introduces no new benchmark or experiments.

COVERAGE: All 92 pages of the PDF were extracted, 380,100 chars. I read pages 1-52 (body, conclusion) and 81-92 (appendices A-F) in full. Pages 53-80 are the reference list. I did not read it line by line, only the origins visible in the text. The relevance note was not re-read after I saw its header, and I did not check it for existing world-model coverage. Figure captions are taken from the extracted text, not from the figures script.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The paper's core taxonomy has three capability levels. L1 Predictor learns one-step transitions, L2 Simulator composes them into multi-step, action-conditioned rollouts that respect domain laws, and L3 Evolver revises its own model from evidence.
  number: none (3 levels x 4 law regimes: physical, digital, social, scientific)
  setup: Conceptual framework over >400 works and >100 systems. The levels describe capability, not model types.
  quote: "L1 Predictor, which learns one-step local transition operators;L2 Simulator, which composes them into multi-step, action-conditioned rollouts that respect domain laws; andL3 Evolver, which autonomously revises its own model when predictions fail against new evidence."
  where: p1 abstract

- claim: Agent-runtime view. One deployed agent moves between levels depending on the task. L1 handles reactive one-step prediction. L2 is used when comparing candidate action sequences. L3 is invoked when failures cannot be fixed by re-planning. L3 is a governance layer, not a replacement for L1/L2.
  number: none
  setup: Conceptual. The paper says the world model is one component beside tool use, memory, multi-agent coordination and reflection.
  quote: "This runtime dispatch view clarifies why L3 is not a replacement for L1/L2 but a governance layer that improves the stack when evidence demands it."
  where: p6

- claim: L2 has three boundary conditions: long-horizon coherence, intervention sensitivity, constraint consistency. Closed-loop use (planning) is orthogonal to the levels. A model that predicts well one step ahead but fails any of these is still L1.
  number: none
  quote: "A model that predicts the next step accurately yet collapses under composition, ignores action edits, or violates domain rules remains better understood as L1 with strong local prediction, rather than as a full L2 simulator."
  where: p12-13, p21

- claim: L3 is defined by three boundary conditions (evidence-grounded diagnosis, persistent asset update, governed validation with rollback/canary). Update loop: design, execute, observe, reflect. A loop alone is not L3. Evidence must become persistent, regression-checked updates (skills, rules, parsers, tests), not in-context patches.
  number: none
  quote: "Persistent asset update:fixes are promoted as reusable assets (skills, rules, parsers, tests), not only ephemeral in-context patches." and "Governed validation:updates pass regression and robustness gates (including rollback and canary policies) before default enablement."
  where: p13; p31

- claim: Five recurring L2 failure modes: compounding error, state aliasing/drift, controllability failure, exploitability/simulator escape, calibration failure under distribution shift. Best mitigation for compounding error is shorter planning windows with frequent replanning on real feedback, not better one-step predictions.
  number: none
  quote: "The most effective mitigations are not making one-step predictions look better, but shortening effective planning windows (decomposing long tasks into verifiable short segments and replanning frequently with real feedback)"; "In practice, confident but wrong should be treated as a strong signal for evolution"
  where: p30

- claim: Making constraints explicit and checkable improves long-horizon stability more than raising perceptual fidelity. Hard constraint layers belong at inference time, not learned softly.
  number: none
  quote: "Making constraints explicit (loggable, replayable, regressable) often improves long-horizon stability more than increasing perceptual fidelity."; "separate what is learned from what is enforced: hard constraint layers (collision checkers, state-machine validators, regression gates) should be applied at inference time rather than learned implicitly"
  where: p30; p47

- claim: Evaluate world models by decision quality, not generative metrics. Two proposed metrics are Action Success Rate (ASR) and Counterfactual Outcome Deviation (COD). Low COD means the model ignores actions and is useless for counterfactual planning.
  number: formulas only
  quote: "The relevant bridge is therefore not “Does the model look realistic?” but “Does improved model validity change what the agent chooses, and does that shift in choice in turn improve real-world task outcomes?”"; "When COD is low, a world model is largely unresponsive to changes in action"
  where: p39

- claim: Most systems are evaluated only at L1. L2-style protocols are not standard. L3 evaluation infrastructure is essentially absent outside autonomous science.
  number: none
  quote: "L3 evaluation infrastructure (regression suites, asset validation gates, cross-episode improvement tracking) is essentially nonexistent outside autonomous science."
  where: p42

- claim: Minimal Reproducible Evaluation Package (MREP) proposed: version locking, trace logs, failure taxonomy, tail statistics (bootstrap CIs, IQM), boundary-condition mapping. Components needing new infrastructure are automated failure taxonomy and boundary mapping.
  number: five components
  quote: "Trace Logs:Full logs of intermediate steps, including observations, actions, and receipts, sufficient to replay and attribute failures post hoc."
  where: p90

- claim: L3 maturity differs by regime. Scientific is "Established", digital "Partial", physical "Emerging", social "Aspirational". Digital L3 (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, CodeIt) usually lacks active experiment design. Governance risks are benchmark overfitting, knowledge contamination, misattribution cascades.
  number: none
  quote: "Benchmark overfittingoccurs when the regression gate is too close to the training distribution; the system learns to pass tests rather than improve genuinely."
  where: p38

- claim: Autonomous-lab evidence for L3. A-Lab ran 17 days closed-loop and made 36 compounds from 57 targets in 353 experiments. CAMEO found a phase-change memory material without extra human training.
  number: 17 days, 353 experiments, 36 of 57 targets
  setup: Robotic synthesis plus XRD with active learning (Szymanski et al. 2023). Figures are reported by the survey, not re-measured.
  quote: "In 17 days of closed-loop operation, A-Lab performed 353 experiments and realized 36 compounds from 57 targets."
  where: p35

- claim: Code and tool-calling world models. SWE-World lifts a 32B coder from 6.2% to 52.0% on SWE-bench Verified using a learned execution surrogate. CWM (32B) reaches 65.8% on SWE-bench Verified with test-time scaling. A foresight study warns that agents rarely invoke simulators and can degrade.
  number: 6.2% to 52.0%; 65.8%
  setup: SWE-bench Verified, as reported by the survey from other papers.
  quote: "lifting a 32B coder from 6.2% to 52.0% on SWE-bench Verified"; "agents rarely invoke simulation, frequently misuse predicted rollouts, and can even degrade in performance"
  where: p25, p27

- claim: Tool-calling agents can use a world model as a rollout engine to predict a call's outcome before committing. Examples are GTM (a simulator trained on >20,000 tools) and DyMo (state prediction during function calling, which cut hallucinations on BFCL V2).
  number: >20,000 tools
  quote: "with training data synthesized across more than 20,000 tools"
  where: p26-27

- claim: Web-agent world models. Off-the-shelf LLMs are not enough as web world models. DreamGym gave >30% on WebArena. WebWorld was trained on >1M trajectories and supports 30+ step simulation.
  number: >30%; >1M trajectories
  quote: "achieving over 30% improvement on WebArena"
  where: p25

- claim: Theory-of-mind and social simulation are weak. ExploreToM accuracy is as low as 9% for GPT-4o. LLMs degrade beyond second-order beliefs. Only 2 of 15 LLMs sustain cooperation in a commons dilemma.
  number: 9%; 2 of 15
  quote: "ExploreToM (Sclar et al., 2024) achieves accuracy as low as 9% for GPT-4o"; "Only 2 of 15 LLMs achieve sustainable cooperation in commons dilemma scenarios"
  where: p27, p85

- claim: Physical-consistency gap. The best of twelve frontier video models reaches only 0.262 on conservation-law and object-permanence probes.
  number: 0.262
  setup: PhyWorldBench (Gu et al. 2025a), reported by the survey.
  quote: "the best of twelve frontier models attains only a 0.262 success rate on conservation-law and object-permanence probes"
  where: p49

- claim: Weather surrogates beat the operational system. GraphCast and Pangu-Weather beat ECMWF on 90% of verification targets. GenCast beats the ensemble on 97.2%.
  number: 90%; 97.2%
  quote: "outperform the ECMWF operational system on 90% of verification targets"; "outperforming the ensemble system on 97.2% of targets"
  where: p28

- claim: Latency budgets per regime. Robotics <100ms, driving <200ms, web/GUI ~1-5s, software engineering ~5-30s, social ~1-10s, science minutes to hours. Social simulation pairwise belief updates scale O(n^2).
  number: see list
  setup: Deployment budget ranges, "not measured benchmark results".
  quote: "These are deployment budget ranges rather than measured benchmark results"
  where: p46

- claim: Harness engineering is framed as world modeling for software agents. The progression runs prompt, context, then harness engineering.
  number: none
  quote: "harness engineering designs the executable environment surrounding the model: tools, memory, feedback loops, and inter-agent topology"
  where: p50 (open problem 10)

- claim: Attack results on world models are preliminary. PhysCond-WMA reports 55% targeted success. JailWAM reports 84.2% on LingBot-VA. The survey says these await replication.
  number: 55%; 84.2%
  quote: "These attack studies are recent preprints from a small set of overlapping author groups whose findings await independent replication"
  where: p51

- claim: Worked L3 examples in Appendix D (grasp friction, cancellation strategy, installation skill, materials) are constructive illustrations, not deployed results. The installation example (error, attribute to permission failure, make a skill template plus regression test, replay on OSWorld) is the closest to an agent-engineering pattern.
  number: the cancellation example uses 20% vs 70% predicted retention over 50 dialogues (hypothetical)
  quote: "These are constructive illustrations, not reports of deployed system behavior."
  where: p87-88

LIMITS
- Authors concede: early-access preprint, not peer reviewed, "may be inaccurate or incomplete" (p1). Philosophical analogies are "heuristic rather than historical or one-to-one" (p8). Level boundaries are judgment-based, and real systems mix regimes.
- No new experiments. All numbers are secondhand from cited papers. Setups are often not given.
- L3 support is uneven. Social, code and embodied L3 are "partly empirical and partly prospective" (p33).
- Attack and security figures are from unreplicated preprints.
- Appendix D cases are hypothetical.
- Compounding error and "O(1)" claims are qualitative. The survey notes the constant factor matters (p91).
- The word "agent" appears throughout, but this is not a general agent-architecture paper. It covers the predictive substrate only.
- Dating: the source cites 2025-2026 preprints (Genie 3, SWE-World, Web World Models, RAGEN-2). Benchmark scores will move.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Ha and Schmidhuber 2018 (World Models); Hafner et al. 2019, 2020, 2021, 2025 (PlaNet/Dreamer family); Schrittwieser et al. 2020 (MuZero); Sutton 1991; Kaelbling et al. 1998 (POMDP); LeCun 2022 (JEPA architecture); Pearl 2009 (causal hierarchy); Moerland et al. 2023 (MBRL survey); Friston 2010; Lewis 1973; Lakatos 1978; Popper 1959; Kuhn 1962; Duhem and Quine. Competing surveys: Ding et al. 2025a; Zhu et al. 2024; Yue et al. 2025. For L3: Lu et al. 2024a (AI Scientist), Romera-Paredes et al. 2024 (FunSearch), Novikov et al. 2025 (AlphaEvolve), Kusne et al. 2020 (CAMEO), Szymanski et al. 2023 (A-Lab), Sparkes et al. 2010 (Robot Scientist Adam). For agents: Yao et al. 2022 (WebShop/ReAct era), Gu et al. 2025b (WebDreamer), Yang et al. 2024a (SWE-agent), Park et al. 2023 (Generative Agents), Wang et al. 2024b (Voyager), Xie et al. 2024 (OSWorld), Jimenez et al. 2024 (SWE-bench). Also Anthropic 2025 (context engineering) and Rajasekaran 2026 / Pan et al. 2026 (harness engineering).

CODE: none. The paper has no code. Formal snippets worth keeping:
- L2 query (p21): p̂(τ|z0,a1:H,c) ∝ ∏ pθ(zt|zt-1,at) · φc(τ). The constraint term φc couples the whole trajectory, so it does not factor per step.
- L3 loop (p31): Mt –design→ at –execute→ ot –observe→ dt –reflect→ Mt+1.
- ASR = (1/N) Σ 1[task_i succeeds under policy derived from p̂] (p39).

FIGURES (captions from extracted text)
- Fig 5, p8: hierarchy L1 Predictor, L2 Simulator, L3 Evolver, Beyond L3. Quick visual of the levels.
- Fig 7, p10: unified POMDP graphical model, with scopes of L1, L2, L3 marked. Shows that L3 is the reflect arrow Mt to Mt+1.
- Fig 8, p29: diagnostic map of the four regimes by formalizability and observability, with constraints and failures per regime.
- Fig 9, p32: L3 loop of design, execute, observe, reflect, with anomaly vs epistemic gap triggers.
- Fig 10, p34: L3 across four regimes, with maturity labels Emerging, Partial, Aspirational, Established.
- Tables 4, 7, 9, 12, 13 carry the compact comparisons (boundary conditions by regime, failures by regime, revision signals, latency budgets, design roadmap). Table 9 (p37) lists the revision signals that trigger L3 updates per regime.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean text. Tables are flattened and check marks render as symbols. Some words are run together, such as "termworld modelcarries".
- Table 9 row colours (falsifiability) are lost in extraction.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF text.
- Relevance caution for the caller. The note's stated scope is "Agent = LLM + Context + Tools", the ReAct loop, and workflow vs agent choice. This source is a world-model taxonomy. It sharpens the note mainly on four points: (a) L3 as governed self-improvement with regression gates, rollback and canary, (b) world-model-as-tool-simulator before committing a call, (c) the "when to simulate" caveat, (d) harness engineering. I did not read the note beyond its header, so I did not check whether it already covers these points.
- Text copy is at /tmp/chu/t.txt, with page markers like [[p12]].
